newsitem.title: USA: Germany wants new world trade round from 2000.
newsitem.headline: Germany wants new world trade round from 2000.

text.p: Rejecting U.S. calls for a piece-meal approach to world trade, Germany said Saturday it wanted a broad new round of talks on liberalizing global commerce to start from the year 2000.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, speaking at the Denver summit of G7 leading industrial nations, said Washington was wrong to insist on liberalizing world trade in narrow sectors like lumber exports or trade in fishery products.
He indicated Germany, one of the stronger proponents of freer world trade in the European Union, saw the U.S. approach as a way to win an unfair advantage for American business.
"If we liberalize in sectors where only a few have an advantage, that's not the right way," he told journalists. "That leads to a dead end."
"From the year 2000, we want a global trade liberalization round to take place, with a global rather than a sectoral approach."
Global trade reform talks, which would be held under the 128-member World Trade Organisation (WTO), often take years to conclude and highlight deep tensions between different trading states or blocs.
The last major trade talks, the so-called Uruguay Round, lasted from 1986 to 1993 and almost collapsed several times over disputes between the European Union and the U.S.

Since then, separate deals on information technology and telecommunications have helped integrate world trade in those front-line sectors. WTO members have singled out farm produce and textiles as two further sectors that could be opened up.
Rexrodt noted the information technology deal had helped all countries involved but questioned U.S. efforts to liberalize commerce in more restricted areas.
"The Americans are now talking about wood and fishery products," he said. "That is not the main point for us and for other countries."

Germany wanted its point of view to be reflected in the final communiqe of the annual G7 summit, which this year included Russia in all but a brief economic session for the first time, but it would not be expressed that clearly, he added.
The G7 includes the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada.

On another trade issue, Rexrodt said Germany firmly backed Russia's bid to become a member of the Geneva-based WTO and thought China, which wants to join but is caught in a struggle with Taiwan about who should go first, should also come in.

But both states, once rival leaders of a communist world that competed with the western industrial states that are now their main trading partners, would have to respect the WTO's tariff-cutting and market-opening rules.
"Being a member of the WTO while not respecting the rules will not be possible," he said.
"We want open markets and trade to remain an impulse for the world economy," he said. "We Germans want a general reduction of trade barriers around the world."
